title: Real Time
logline: Tom wants everything real time, and Marcus learns that fast data is only worth having when it is also correct, affordable and still standing when a region goes dark.

modules.logline: A text-to-SQL bot embarrasses the CEO, and Marcus learns that an answer is only as good as the meaning, permissions and scores behind it.
scenes: The board numbers finally match, and Tom is already back with a new ask: a chat bot that answers any question from the warehouse. Marcus sketches the pieces on a whiteboard. Where does the model end and the data begin?

In Monday's leadership meeting, the CEO asks the bot for last week's Bengaluru revenue. It answers in four seconds, confidently, and double counts every split payment. The room goes quiet. How do you make generated SQL trustworthy?

Marcus reads the bot's query log. It joined trips to payments on the wrong key because "revenue" means three things in three tables. Kofi says the definitions already exist in dbt. Can the bot read them?
Lena notices the bot connects with a service account that can drop tables. Dev asks, flatly, who approved that. Marcus wants the bot to have tools, not passwords. What would an MCP server change?

Operations wants every rider complaint tagged by topic, forty thousand a week. Lena proposes a Python script that calls a model row by row. Marcus wonders whether the warehouse can do it in SQL. What does each row cost?

Asha agrees to a second demo on one condition: show her the score first. Marcus has fifty real questions from finance and no way to grade the answers. How do you evaluate a data agent before it meets the CEO again?
teasers: The CEO asks the bot a simple question in front of everyone. How do you make its SQL trustworthy?
The query log shows why "revenue" broke the bot. Can the bot read your metric definitions?
Lena finds what the bot's database account may drop. What would an MCP server change?
Forty thousand complaints a week and nobody reads them. What does each row cost to classify?
Asha sets one condition for a second demo. How do you evaluate a data agent first?
Next week: a driver sees two wallet balances a minute apart. Which reads must see their own writes?
modules.boss: Incident review: the CEO's double-counted revenue answer. Walk Asha through the guarded SQL, the semantic layer, the read-only tool and the eval score that would have caught it before the meeting.
modules.finale: The second demo scores 46 out of 50, and the bot says "I don't know" for the rest. Grace's advice: "Never ship an answer you cannot grade." That night, two Postgres replicas disagree about a driver's balance.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "Can your robot answer questions?" Marcus says: "Only if we teach it what our words mean and check its homework before anyone sees it."

modules.logline: A wallet bug turns into a split-brain incident, and Marcus goes back to how storage, replication and consensus really work.
scenes: Marcus volunteers for the wallet-balance postmortem and stalls on the first line. Why do payments live in Postgres while ride events sit in an LSM-based store? He realises he has never asked how either engine stores a row.
The timeline is clear now: the driver topped up on the primary, then read from a replica eleven seconds behind. Dev calls it normal. Marcus calls it a bug. Which reads must see their own writes?

Partitioning by city looked tidy until Bengaluru, with 80% of trips, landed on one shard. That shard runs hot every evening while thirteen others idle. How do you spread data without losing what belongs together?

Lena reproduces a rarer bug: two refunds approved for one order, both reading the same balance. Postgres was running read committed. Would a stricter isolation level have stopped it, and at what price?

Then the real incident surfaces. During a network blip, two database nodes each believed they were primary for ninety seconds and both accepted writes. How does a cluster agree on one leader, and whose clock wins?
As the fix rolls out, the driver dashboard's cache key expires and every request hits Postgres at once. The database falls over for four minutes. What should sit between users and the database?
teasers: An eleven-second gap explains two balances. Which reads must see their own writes?
Bengaluru crushes one shard while thirteen idle. How do you spread data and keep what belongs together?
One order, two refunds, one balance read twice. Would a stricter isolation level have stopped it?
For ninety seconds Meridian has two primaries. How does a cluster agree on one leader?
A cache key expires and the database falls over. What should sit between users and the database?
Next week: surge prices per zone every ten seconds. How does Kafka store and hand out messages?
modules.boss: Incident review: the split-brain wallet incident. Asha wants the full chain: replica lag, the isolation level, the failed leader election and the cache stampede that followed. Explain each layer as you would to an interviewer.
modules.finale: The postmortem ships with Dev's name beside Marcus's. Grace reads it over Friday coffee: "Every data tool is a storage engine with opinions." On Monday, Tom arrives with a slide titled Surge Pricing, Live.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "Why did the app say two numbers?" Marcus says: "We keep copies of the notebook, and one copy was a few seconds behind."

modules.logline: Surge pricing moves onto Kafka and Spark streaming, and Marcus learns that data which never stops brings late events, duplicates and poison messages.
scenes: Tom wants surge multipliers per zone, recalculated every ten seconds from live trip requests. The batch job runs hourly. Marcus lists what changes when data never stops: late events, no natural end. Why is streaming harder than batch?

Dev draws the trip-request topic: 48 partitions, keyed by zone. Lena asks why one consumer lags while the others idle. The answer is inside Kafka. How does it actually store, order and hand out messages?

In testing, a rider in Koramangala is charged surge twice for one request. The consumer crashed after writing but before committing its offset. At least once or exactly once: which guarantee does pricing really need?

Marcus rebuilds the surge job in Spark Structured Streaming with ten-second windows. Then a phone that lost signal uploads requests from twenty minutes ago. Should a late event change a price already shown?
The mobile team renames a field in the trip event without telling anyone. The streaming job keeps running, but surge in every zone drops to 1.0. How should a stream handle a schema that changes?
Friday, 11 p.m.: Nadia leaves for a night shift, Zoe is asleep, and Marcus is on call. The pager fires: one malformed message, consumer lag climbing past two million. Retry it, skip it, or park it?
teasers: One consumer drowns while its neighbours idle. How does Kafka hand out messages?
A rider pays surge twice for one ride. Which delivery guarantee does pricing really need?
Twenty-minute-old requests arrive from a phone that lost signal. Should a late event change a shown price?
Someone renames a field and surge drops to 1.0 everywhere. How should a stream handle schema change?
A night shift, a sleeping child and a pager that will not stop. Retry it, skip it or park it?
Next week: refunds in Postgres and the warehouse disagree. How does log-based capture work?
modules.boss: Incident review: the poison message and the two-million-message lag. Dev wants the timeline, the dead-letter design, the guarantee pricing truly needs, and whether Flink, Spark or Kafka Streams should own surge next year.
modules.finale: Surge runs live in all fourteen cities, with a dead-letter topic and a lag alert. Nadia asks him to swap his next on-call week. Grace: "Choose the weakest guarantee the business can live with." Then finance flags mismatched refunds.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "What is a stream?" Marcus says: "A conveyor belt of little notes that never stops, so we add them up as they pass."

modules.logline: Refunds in Postgres and the warehouse disagree, and change data capture finally explains the 2% revenue gap from Marcus's first month.
scenes: Finance reports that October refunds in Postgres total more than refunds in Snowflake. Lena pulls up last year's month-end close: the same 2% revenue gap. The nightly export copies rows, but does it copy every change?

Marcus traces it: the export selects rows by updated_at, so refunds edited after the cut-off and rows deleted outright never arrive. Dev suggests reading the Postgres write-ahead log instead. How does log-based capture work?

Debezium now streams every change into Kafka. Each insert, update and delete must land in the Iceberg table once, in order. Lena asks what a delete even looks like in a lake. How do you apply changes to a table?
Kofi wants refunds on his dashboard within seconds. Marcus writes the same CDC job in Flink SQL, and it fits on one screen. But is shorter also correct when updates for one order arrive out of order?
The pipeline runs, and the totals still differ by 0.3%. Asha asks how anyone will know the numbers match tomorrow. Marcus needs a check that proves it every day. What do you count, and where?

The last causes are dull and real: refunds issued weeks after a trip, and a replication slot that once filled the disk. Lena proposes an agent that drafts the backfill. Who approves it before it runs?
teasers: The nightly export misses every change after the cut-off. How does log-based capture work?
Debezium arrives and Lena asks what a delete looks like in a lake. How do you apply changes?
Kofi wants refunds in seconds through Flink SQL. Is shorter also correct when updates arrive out of order?
The pipeline runs and the totals are still 0.3% apart. What do you count, and where?
The last clue to the 2% gap is weeks old. Who approves a fix before it runs?
Next week: at 3 a.m. the right runbook is nowhere. How should documents be chunked?
modules.boss: Incident review: the database and the warehouse disagree. Present the whole 2% story to Asha and finance: missed deletes, late refunds, the full slot, the CDC design and the daily reconciliation that now guards it.
modules.finale: For the first time since Marcus joined, the month closes with a difference of zero. Lena presents the fix herself. Grace: "Trust is a reconciliation you run every day." Then the on-call channel asks for help again.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "Did you find the lost money?" Marcus says: "It was never lost; we missed some changes, so now we write down every change as it happens."

modules.logline: On-call wants a bot that answers from runbooks, and Marcus treats retrieval as a data pipeline that must stay fresh, private and measured.
scenes: At 3 a.m. Lena is on call, the lag alert fires, and the fix sits in a runbook four pages deep in wiki search. Dev wants a bot that answers from runbooks. Marcus says it is a data pipeline first. Why?

The first prototype splits runbooks every 500 characters. Asked how to drain the dead-letter topic, it returns half a command and a heading from another page. How should documents be chunked and embedded?
Mei asks why the team needs a new vector database bill. Marcus checks whether Postgres with pgvector, or even DuckDB, could hold forty thousand chunks. Where should the vectors live?
Dev updates the CDC runbook after Tuesday's change, but a week later the bot still recommends the old command. On call, a stale answer is worse than none. How do you keep an index fresh?
Lena wants to load two years of postmortems too. Marcus finds rider phone numbers and driver names inside them. Can a model extract the useful parts as ETL without carrying personal data along?
Dev asks the question that matters: how often is the bot right? Marcus has anecdotes, not a number. How do you measure retrieval and answers separately, and when should the bot say it does not know?
teasers: The bot answers with half a command and the wrong heading. How should runbooks be chunked?
Mei asks why forty thousand chunks need their own database. Where should the vectors live?
A runbook changed last week and the bot did not notice. How do you keep an index fresh?
Two years of postmortems, full of phone numbers. Can extraction leave personal data behind?
Dev wants a number for how often the bot is right. How do you measure retrieval and answers apart?
Next week: the AI bill jumps fourfold. Why does the first word take so long?
modules.boss: Incident review: the on-call bot that gave a stale command at 3 a.m. Show Dev the pipeline: chunking, the fresh index, redaction, citations, the abstain rule and the retrieval score that would have flagged it.
modules.finale: The runbook bot now cites its sources and abstains when unsure, and Lena's next shift ends early. Grace: "Measure retrieval before you touch the prompt." Then Mei forwards the model invoice with one word: why?
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "How does the robot know?" Marcus says: "It finds the right page in our instruction books first, reads it out, and says when it is not sure."

modules.logline: Model costs quadruple and answers slow to nine seconds, and Marcus puts a gateway, traces, evals and guardrails in front of every AI call.
scenes: The model bill is four times last month's, and the text-to-SQL bot now takes nine seconds to answer. Mei wants to know who pays. Marcus wants to know where the time goes. What changes once AI is in production?
Tracing one slow request, Marcus finds most of the nine seconds pass before the first token: a 30,000-token prompt stuffed with the whole schema. What is the model server doing while the user waits?

Mei builds a spreadsheet: input tokens, output tokens, retries, and three teams using the largest model for simple tagging. Every request has a price. Which changes make it cheaper and faster without making it worse?
Five teams call three model providers with five keys and no shared limits. One retry loop caused half the spike. Dev proposes a single LLM gateway in front of everything. What must the gateway own?

Lena moves the complaint tagger to a smaller model and costs drop 70%. Kofi asks whether the tags are still right. Nobody knows, because nothing scores answers in production. How do you keep score live?
A rider types a card number into the support bot, and it appears in a trace log. Asha wants guardrails before the next launch. Where in the request path do the checks belong?
teasers: A nine-second answer, mostly before the first word. What is the model server doing meanwhile?
Mei prices every request and three teams look expensive. Which changes cut cost without hurting answers?
Five teams, three providers, five keys and one retry loop. What must a gateway own?
The cheaper model saves 70%. How do you know the answers are still right?
A card number shows up in a log. Where in the request path do the checks belong?
Next week: the move to AWS begins. How does S3 behave under the familiar paths?
modules.boss: Incident review: the fourfold AI bill and the nine-second bot. Walk Mei and Asha through the traces, the cost per request, the gateway's limits and caching, the eval gate and the guardrails that close the gaps.
modules.finale: The bill falls below last quarter's and the bot answers in under two seconds. Grace: "Put a price on every request before anyone asks." Then Asha announces the data centre lease ends in March: Meridian moves to AWS.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "Why is the robot expensive?" Marcus says: "Every word it reads costs a little, so we taught it to read less and use a smaller brain for easy jobs."

modules.logline: Meridian moves its platform to AWS while Mei watches the bill triple, and launch night ends with a region going dark.
scenes: Asha gives the team one quarter to move the platform to AWS. Tom asks whether streaming moves too. Marcus maps what changes and what stays the same: tables and jobs stay, storage, access and bills change. Where is the real risk?
Lena copies the lake to S3, and the first Spark job crawls, listing millions of tiny files. Dev asks about versioning and lifecycle rules. How does S3 really behave underneath the familiar paths?
Reviewing permissions, Marcus finds the Airflow role can read every bucket, payments included, through a wildcard. Nobody remembers why. How do you give each job only the access it needs in IAM?
Should the nightly batch run on EMR, Glue or containers on ECS, and who schedules it? Dev wants clusters he understands; Mei wants nothing running at 3 p.m. What decides the compute choice?
Two engineers click the same staging setup into existence by hand, and a job works in one and fails in the other. Marcus insists on Terraform. Can the whole batch path live as reviewed code?
Three weeks in, Mei posts the bill: triple the old data centre. Cross-zone transfer, idle clusters, a NAT gateway carrying every S3 read. Her question is short: who pays for this, and why?
teasers: The first Spark job on S3 spends its time listing files. How does S3 really behave?
A wildcard role can read the payments bucket. How does each job get only what it needs?
Dev wants clusters and Mei wants nothing running at 3 p.m. What decides the compute choice?
Two hand-built staging setups behave differently. Can the batch path live as reviewed code?
The first full AWS bill is triple the estimate. Who pays for it, and why?
Next season: Meridian is buying Lumen. Can Marcus read Victor's Scala by Friday?
modules.boss: Incident review: the bill triples and a role is too broad. Show Mei and Asha the cost breakdown, the fixes for transfer and idle compute, the narrowed IAM roles and the Terraform that keeps them narrow.
modules.finale: Launch night: every pipeline runs on AWS and the dashboards are green. Grace texts: "Test the failover before you need it." At 1:40 a.m. the pager fires. A whole region is dark, and surge has stopped.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks: "What is the cloud?" Marcus says: "A huge computer room we rent by the minute, so we must remember to switch the lights off."
